items.title: Today's lesson
items.content:
A turmeric stain turning reddish-brown under soap, and a remedy for acidity, open the lesson.

**Indicator colours** sort acids from bases; zinc, carbonates and copper oxide show **how acids react**, and zinc, carbon dioxide and phenolphthalein **how bases react**.

A bulb test reveals the **ions** behind it all; we close with the safe way to **dilute an acid**.

items.title: You already know
items.content:
• writing and balancing equations with state symbols

• displacement, double displacement and the reactivity series

• ions and their charges; exothermic reactions

items.title: By the end, you can
items.content:
**1.** Identify acids and bases with indicators.

**2.** Write the reactions of acids with metals, carbonates and metal oxides.

**3.** Write the reactions of bases, including neutralisation.

**4.** Explain what all acids and all bases have in common.

**5.** Explain why acid is added to water when diluting.

**What this shows**

Four indicators, each tested with dilute hydrochloric acid (left column) and dilute sodium hydroxide solution (right column).

**Answer to Question 3**

**Acid**: blue litmus turns red, red litmus stays red, phenolphthalein stays colourless, methyl orange turns red.

**Base**: red litmus turns blue, blue litmus stays blue, phenolphthalein turns pink, methyl orange turns yellow.

items.prompt: You have three test tubes: distilled water, an acid and a base. You have only red litmus paper. How will you identify each?
options: Find the base (red → blue), then test the other two with that blue paper
Find the acid (red → blue), then test the other two with that blue paper
Find the base (red → blue); water and the acid cannot be told apart
It cannot be done: red litmus changes only in a base

items.text:
**On this question**

Dip red litmus in each: the one that turns it **blue** is the base. Dip this blue paper in the other two: the acid turns it **red**; water leaves it blue.

items.text:
**What this shows**

Black copper oxide stirred into dilute hydrochloric acid: (a) at the start, (b) after stirring for a while.

**Answer to Question 7**

It has **dissolved**:

$\mathrm{CuO}$ + $\mathrm{2HCl}$ $\longrightarrow$ $\mathrm{CuCl_{2}}$ + $\mathrm{H_{2}O}$

Copper(II) chloride makes the solution blue-green.

items.text:
**Answer to Question 8**

**Hydrogen.**

$\mathrm{2NaOH(aq)}$ + $\mathrm{Zn(s)}$ $\longrightarrow$ $\mathrm{Na_{2}ZnO_{2}}$ + $\mathrm{H_{2}(g)}$

$\mathrm{Na_2ZnO_2}$ is sodium zincate.

items.text:
**What this shows**

NaOH solution with phenolphthalein (pink); after dilute HCl is added drop by drop; after a few more drops of NaOH.

**Answer to Question 9**

The acid uses up the base, so the solution is no longer basic and phenolphthalein turns **colourless**. Extra NaOH makes it basic again: **pink**.

items.prompt: Which pair gives only a salt and water?

items.text:
**On this question**

**C**: a base and a non-metal oxide give a salt $\mathrm{(CaCO_3)}$ and water. **A** and **D** also give hydrogen; **B** also gives $\mathrm{CO_2}$.

items.text:
**What this shows**

The same circuit, a battery, a bulb and two electrodes, dipped in dilute hydrochloric acid and in glucose solution.

**Answer to Question 10**

**Ions.** The acid solution has ions; glucose solution has none, so glucose is not an acid.

**Answer to Question 11**

$\mathrm{H^{+}}$ ions form **only in water**. Dry HCl gas has no $\mathrm{H^{+}}$ ions.

items.prompt: How does the concentration of hydronium ions change when an acid is diluted?
options: It decreases: the same ions spread through more water
It increases: water adds more $\mathrm{H_3O^{+}}$ ions
It stays the same: the number of ions does not change
It falls to zero: water neutralises the acid

items.text:
**On this question**

**A**: the same $\mathrm{H_3O^{+}}$ ions are spread through more water.
